CHAPTER THREE

*The harbour keeps its own count of the boats that never come back, and it does not share the number.*
—from *The Tidewater Almanac*, by Orla Vance

The ferry was late again, and the rain had found its way under the awning where Petra stood with her suitcase pressed against her knees.

"You'll want the second pier," said the man at the ticket window, without looking up from his ledger. "The first one floods when the tide turns."

"It isn't turning yet," Petra said.

"It always is, if you wait long enough." He tore the ticket along its perforation and slid it under the glass. "Second pier. Mind the gulls; they think the bread is theirs."

She did not have any bread, but she thanked him anyway and walked out along the boards, counting the lamps as she went, because her grandmother had told her that a harbour with an even number of lamps was an honest one.

"Seven," said a voice behind her, and she turned to find a boy of perhaps twelve carrying a coil of rope over one shoulder. "Everyone counts them. There used to be eight."

"What happened to the eighth?"

"Storm took it, the year before I was born. My father says the harbour master never replaced it so that people would keep asking." He grinned, as though the question were a coin she had paid him. "You're going across to the island, then?"

"To my aunt's house," Petra said. "If the ferry ever arrives."

"It will," the boy said, and pointed into the grey, where a low shape had begun to separate itself from the rain. "It always does, if you wait long enough."
